In any workplace, good lighting is more than important, it is essential. Lighting should allow people to see clearly so they can work safely. Things we ought to consider when deciding on the adequacy of lighting are:
- how much light there is in an area
- how many lights there are, the type of lights and where they are placed
- what work activities are performed in the area

If an area is well-lit, employees should easily be able see both their work and work environment. If they need to strain their eyes to see, then it's time to have the lighting upgraded. It's important to remember that not all activities require the same level or quality of light. Have someone look at the tasks performed in an area to determine the lighting needs. An activity not requiring high visual acuity shouldn't require optimum quality or level of lighting. However, drawing, document checking, and other fine detailed work requiring more than moderate work with your eyes does.

Since our eyes adapt quickly to lighting conditions, we see well in most lighting levels. When you walk from a bright room into a darker one, your eyes allow you to see clearly in the new light level within a few seconds. Getting lights installed in the workplace that reduce demands on the eyes when people are moving from area to area is the best scenario. By having lighting installed to address this, you are helping your employees work in a brighter, safer environment.

Causative Get and Have: Get + -ed: Active and Passive
You use get and have in both active and passive structures.
The active pattern conveys the meaning of ‘cause or order someone to do something'. The form is:

get + person + to - infinitive OR
have + person + infinitive without to

For example:
I'll get the secretary to put in an order.
I'll have the secretary put in an order.

The passive pattern conveys the meaning of ‘arrange somebody else to do something'. The form is:

get/have + object + past participle

For example:
I will have/get my car fixed.
In this case, it means that somebody else will fix the car.

Using the Modals Shall, Ought to and Should to Ask For Advice
You use the modals should and ought to to express your opinion about what is right and what is wrong.
When you give advice, you are telling someone what you think is the right thing to do in a certain situation.
The most common modal for giving advice is should.

For example:
You really shouldn't be working so hard - you'll get sick!
You should get some rest over the weekend.

You can use ought to in the same sort of situations, but is sounds much more formal.

For example:
You ought to get some rest over the weekend.

You can use shall to ask for advice.

For example:
What shall I do?
Again, this sounds quite formal.
